content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new contrastive learning task in the supervised setting. The label information for learning representation is introduced in the previous supervised contrastive learning (SCL). Similarly, this paper further extends the similarity label (similar or dissimilar) to the continuous similarity value in [0, 1]. The corresponding loss function is designed. Experiments on vision and language tasks validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

(1). The paper is well-written and easy to understand.

(2). Experiments are very sufficient and the results are also strong.


**Weaknesses:**

(1). The motivation is not solid. I agree with the authors that the continuous similarity label can provide more plentiful supervision during model training. However, such human annotations are much more difficult to obtain than the similarity label (can be obtained from the class annotation). Therefore, I do not think the problem setting proposed in this paper really has good practical usability.

(2). The novelty is limited. I understand that the setting of continuous similarity is new in contrastive learning. However, please note that SCL can also be regarded as a regular similarity learning task (equipped with data augmentation). In similarity learning, there are already the problem settings with continuous similarity supervision [1, 2].

(3). The contribution of Theorem 1 is unclear. Firstly, this is a direct extension of the NT-Xent loss. Second, this result is mainly about the training phase and convergence behavior. I do not think it reveals any good properties, such as improving the final/downstream generalization ability.

(4). The experimental comparisons are unfair. Since LASCon uses more supervision, can we still compare it with the completely unsupervised (self-supervised) learning approaches such as SimCLR? Since we use more supervision, it is not surprising that we can obtain higher acc.

(5). Experiments on mainstream datasets such as STL, CIFAR, and ImageNet are missing.

Ref.:

[1]. Zhang et al., f-Similarity Preservation Loss for Soft Labels: A Demonstration on Cross-Corpus Speech Emotion Recognition, AAAI'19.

[2]. Lin et al., Unsupervised Person Re-identification via Softened Similarity Learning, CVPR'20.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As I discussed in the above strengths and weaknesses, the clarity are relatively good, but I think the novelty is rather limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on the above discussion, I do not think extending SCL to a continuous similarity supervised case is a really useful setting. It is unrealistic to obtain the exact similarity annotaiton in [0, 1], especially for the large-scale datasets. I would like to vote for a "reject". Please correct me if I misunderstand any points.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a generalized loss for supervised contrastive learning with a weight factor that is measured from the similarity of the label domain. The authors conclude the task-specific design of the label similarities and point out that their loss essentially regularizes the alignment and uniformity of the representation space. The paper proposes extensive experiments with wide topics and demonstrates the performance of their loss compared with existing constructive losses.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
This paper focuses on the tasks that have correlations within the label set. The idea that considering the similarity of those labels did not attract much attention in the community before. 

The concluded generalized formula looks reasonable, and the theoretical analysis based on the alignment-uniform theory looks interesting.

This paper widely evaluates their proposed loss on 4 different tasks and demonstrates the efficiency of their proposed losses. 


===========================

Weakness:

The organization of this paper is somehow a mess. This paper does not contain a related work section to summarize the existing contrast learning methods. It’s a question if this is the first work that considers the labeling similarity in constructive learning. The authors probably need to compare their method with more existing works.

The method proposed by this paper has limited scope, such that the specific tasks should contain measurable similarities. The general classification tasks won't benefit from the proposed method.

It's recommended to put the experimental settings of section D1 into the main paper.


===========================

Other minor problems: 

It seems that section 3.3.2 is not completed. 

The formulas after section 3.4 do not have an index.

Why does the supCon result in Figure 2(b) look blank? It needs more discussion.

Why are some citations are anonymous?

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper generalizes the supervised contrastive learning(SupCon) loss function to be aware of label similarity in order to improve the performance on tasks with continuous labels. The proposed method pulls together the representations with a weight in proportion to label similarity instead of equally pulling together representations having the same label. Experiments show that the proposed loss function outperforms self-supervised contrastive learning(SimCLR) and SupCon across different tasks, data types and encoder architectures.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- The topic of extending contrastive learning outside classification tasks(i.e. tasks with hard label) is interesting, and this paper proposes to utilize the similarity of continuous labels in the contrastive loss.
- The proposed extension of contrastive loss is natural and understandable. SimCLR and SupCon are shown to be viewed as particular cases of the proposed loss function.
- The experiments span many domains, including NLP, vision, graph and multimodal. Suitable encoder architectures are chosen, and sufficient hyperparameter values have been searched.
 
Cons:
- Novelty in the paper is not enough. As the authors have mentioned in 2.3, there are already several papers trying to generalize SupCon to be label-similarity-aware, and [Dufumier et al. 2021] has proposed a loss function similar to the loss function used in this paper. Also, most of the analysis in the method description are copies of either [Wang & Isola, 2020] or [Khosla et al. 2020] with trivial extension. Additionally, a question – why do you use an MLP as the predictor instead of a linear head as the contrastive learning frameworks usually do?
 - Theorem 1 is confusing. Where is the definition of “perfect alignment” when there is no (hard) positive pairs? From the proof in appendix we know that the perfectly aligning encoder gives |z_i – z_j| = 0 for each z_i and z_j (actually it should be |z_i – z_j| = 0 for z_i and z_j s.t. s(F(x_i), F(x_j)) != 0), but that means the first term in the loss function pulls together everyone while the second term in the loss function pushes away everyone. Then, what’s the purpose of the theorem? The original theorem in [Wang & Isola, 2020] says their first term pulls together positive pairs(i.e. |z_i – z_j| = 0 for each positive pair z_i and z_j) while their second term pushes away everyone, which makes sense but does not apply to this paper.
 - The baselines used in the experiments are weak. It is not surprising that a supervised method(i.e., the proposed method) will outperform a self-supervised method(i.e., SimCLR), not to mention there are many other self-supervised methods(e.g. BYOL, MoCo v2/v3) have been proposed after SimLR but are ignored by this paper. When compared to SupCon, which is a supervised method, the improvement is very marginal(on CMU-MOSI the correlation is even worse). Moreover, SupCon is designed for classification tasks and not for the regression tasks used in the paper. The paper does not compare with any regression methods, e.g., using a vanilla L1 loss to train the same Encoder + Predictor architecture to directly map the input to the prediction. It neither compares with other label-similarity-aware contrastive loss functions(e.g. those mentioned in 2.3).
 - The empirical analysis for the relationship between performance and alignment or uniformity is not convincing. For example, on Davis dataset, the proposed method has much worse(~50% worse, on IMDB it is only ~30% better) alignment than SupCon, but it can still outperform SupCon. In Figure 3 we can also see many points with bad alignment or uniformity but good performance. Besides, a question – why does your implementation of L_uniform (described in 4.2) omit the log?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is not well written. There are several typos, e.g., the last sentence in 2.1 and the first sentence in 3.4.1 is even truncated. The logical flow in the paper is also confusing. Both 3 and 4 are method sections, and the dataset details are mixed with method description.
 
The paper has marginal novelty. The proposed method is very similar to existing works which deal with specific tasks, so the novelty of this paper lies in investigating the generalized contrastive loss in general regression tasks, but the baselines used in the experiments for general regression tasks are not strong enough.

Most details of the proposed method are presented in the paper, so it should be easy to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper addresses an interesting topic, i.e., generalizing SupCon to tasks with continuous labels. It formulates the label-similarity-aware contrastive loss and evaluates its empirical performance in multiple real-world tasks. However, the method is lack of novelty, the experimental results are not strong enough and the presentation is poor. Therefore, the paper is not ready to be published.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new contrastive objective function for supervised contrastive learning to reflect relative similarity between samples where the similarity is quantified by the label similarity. The proposed loss, Label-similarity Aware Contrastive Loss (LASCon), is defined as a weighted sum of relative similarity loss over all samples with weights defined by the label similarity. The authors consider two types of label similarity functions (linear and tanh) imposed on the difference between the labels. Then, the authors show experimental results on four different types of datasets, NLP, Vision, Graph, Multimodal datasets, and demonstrate that the proposed loss outperforms previous scores with some gains.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

- This paper proposes a new contrastive loss reflecting similarity between samples, quantified by the label similarity.
- This paper shows a potential of this type of contrastive loss in improving the alignment and uniformity of representation.
- Extensive experiments on four different datasets are provided to demonstrate the gain of the proposed method.

Weakness

- The performance of proposed method may highly depend on how the labels are defined on the dataset and how one measures the similarity between labels. The original motivation of this work mentioned by the author was to reflect similarity between samples in defining the contrastive loss. But the proposed method simply uses the ‘numerical difference’ between labels to define the similarity on any pair of samples, which could be misleading in many datasets and applications I guess. 
- The authors provided four datasets/applications where the proposed simple label similarity function can be used in improving the contrastive learning through LASCon. But for all four applications, the gain seems not significant in Table 2.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The idea of this paper is clearly addressed and supported by the experimental results on the considered datasets. Figures and tables may need more explanations--e.g., no explanations for Figure 1, the performance metrics in Table 2 are not defined in the main document, etc.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a new contrastive loss reflecting similarity between samples, quantified by the label similarity, and shows a potential of this type of contrastive loss in improving the alignment and uniformity of representation. However, the performance of proposed method may highly depend on how the labels are defined on the dataset and how one measures the similarity between labels, so I don't think that the proposed loss is a universal loss that can provide gains on different datasets and applications. The original motivation of this work mentioned by the author was to reflect similarity between samples in defining the contrastive loss. But the proposed method simply uses the ‘numerical difference’ between labels to define the similarity on any pair of samples, which could be misleading in many datasets and applications I guess. Even in the four datasets considered in this paper, where the label difference indeed might have similarity information between pairs of samples, the gain from the proposed label-similarity based contrastive loss seems not very significant as shown in Table 2.
